Egorov's Theorem

On a finite-measure set, pointwise convergence is almost uniform. Squeeze the bad set small and the rest converges uniformly.

The slow points hide inside one small set. Remove that set and the rest converges at one pace. The whole space must have finite measure.

For example, of 30 🧑 friends racing to a finish line, one or two may lag; set them aside and the rest arrive at nearly the same pace.

    Any set with uniform convergence must miss all but finitely many spikes, so the discarded set always has infinite measure — which is why Egorov's theorem cannot drop the hypothesis m(X)<∞m(X) < \inftym(X)<∞.

    Contrast the scene's sequence: there the bumps pile up at the single point 0, so deleting a neighborhood of that point suffices.
